title: Tenacious history lover tackles mammoth restoration of 'haunted' Hotel Midway
excerpt: “When I die, I’ll be haunting this hotel. I want whoever is there to be doing a good job caring for it and I'll float around fixing things.”
content:
At the heart of the sleepy Village of Midway is a weathered, two-story wooden building that is a beloved community landmark, and topic of local lore and ghost stories.

The Hotel Midway isn’t just a structure, it has served as a community hub for miners, ranchers and travellers since it was built in 1900, and every knot in the timber and creak in the floorboards is a reminder of its rich history.

When the hotel fell into disrepair a few years ago and was put on the market for a quarter million dollars, creative visionary Carissa Boynton made the purchase and took on the mammoth task of bringing the relic back to life.

“The cost of the motel was so low I knew there’d be a lot of things wrong with it,” Boynton told iNFOnews.ca. “It was a ghost of a building. There was a dormancy about it as it hadn’t been used for a long time. It’d most recently been owned by a cannabis company and used as a residence for workers, and was treated poorly.

“I went to see it with my two oldest sons anyway, and we all fell in love with it and the surrounding area.”

Boynton has former experience hosting guests in the accommodation industry, successfully renting out condos and Airbnbs. Since purchasing the hotel in July, 2023, she has been travelling back and forth to her home and kids in Abbotsford.

It took more than two years of backbreaking renovations and lots of help from the community for Boynton to get the building up to code and open the hotel rooms earlier this year.

“There was a notice on title that it didn’t have occupancy and I had no idea what I was doing, it was my first commercial property,” she said.

“The previous owners had started renovating the fire escape without a building permit which triggered a new building code it had to be brought up to. I spent over two years struggling with that and putting in the new fire escape.”  

Two building permits, three architects, three engineering firms and five contractors were involved in the massive project.

Boynton focussed first on renovating, painting and decorating the six hotel rooms that are located on the top floor, and was able to get them licensed for occupancy in February of this year.

Community members donated furniture, historical items and art to pull it all together, with Boynton sourcing much of her materials from thrift shops and garage sales.

“I call it a vintage boarding house DYI aesthetic,” she said. “I find beauty in worn things and the stories behind them, and I’m focussed on fixing what we already have with more time, creativity and acceptance for things that aren’t perfect.

“The building is all about community and we’re filling up spaces with pieces of interesting history like vintage train photos and a donated organ.”

All of the six renovated rooms have different bedding and decorations, and are of different sizes.

“The room sizes are all inconsistent because that’s how it was built and that’s how it will stay,” Boynton said. “I kept as much as I could of the existing layout, and I’ve added a lot of colour.”

Hotel Midway is associated with memories and local lore, and the biggest story attached to it surrounds the murder of the original proprietor, Charles Thomet, who bought the hotel in the early 1900s and was shot down by bandits shortly after.

Thomet, who was born in Switzerland in 1860 and moved to Portland, Oregon in 1883, was drawn to the boundary country in 1893 by the mining activities happening there, according to an article sent to iNFOnews.ca Kettle Valley Museum curator Wendy Higashi.

He made large land claims in Rock Creek, Midway and Greenwood before visiting Portland again where he met his wife Bertha Zimmerly.

Thomet bought the hotel in 1908 after serving on the Provincial Police Force training bloodhounds and tracking horse and cattle thieves.

After his untimely death, Mrs. Thomet and their five children continued operating the hotel and a reward of $1,000 was posted for the capture of the murderers but they were never found. 

The spooky history prompted paranormal groups to visit the hotel this year to make videos, including an in-depth one by Tracks, Trails and Forgotten Tales.

“Some say Charles still haunts the hotel, looking for his killers,” Boynton said. “I haven’t personally experienced ghost activity here but if there are any they’d be Charles and Bertha, and really excited about what’s happening here.

“When I die, I’ll be haunting this hotel. I want whoever is there to be doing a good job caring for it and I’ll float around fixing things.”

Located at 607 Fifth Avenue, Hotel Midway was the first hotel built in Midway and today is known by some locals as the Midway Hot-L because the “e” on its neon sign fell off decades ago.

Midway is located 50 kilometres east of Osoyoos on Highway 3 in the West Kootenay region of South Central BC on the Kettle River at mile zero of the popular Kettle Valley Rail Trail.

This year Boynton welcomed motorcyclists, hunters and tourists from all over the world. So many cyclists stopped by she made a bike room for safe overnight storage.

Men’s groups and families have booked the entire hotel for occasions, the space hosted numerous community parties and events, and the patio was opened as a beer garden in the summer.

At one point in its history, the hotel had a restaurant and bar in it. Boynton just got the main floor permitted for occupancy and is undergoing talks with authorities to allow the opening of a restaurant and bar.

She keeps friends near and far up-to-date with progress on her Facebook page, which is a community hub of its own with locals sharing fond memories of the hotel.

“I have been learning how to do a lot of things while rebuilding, it has been a labour of love bringing this building back up to speed,” she said. “I enjoy the creativity, the heritage and history, and the welcoming community.”
